---
title: "sapply() does not guarantee the type of what it returns"
ref: DF-01
categories: [Data frames and lists]
impact: silencieux
extrait: 'class(sapply(list(), length))'
reponse: '"list"'
attendu: "an integer vector, possibly empty"
versions: "All"
source: "The R Inferno, hadley/strict"
---

::: {.piege}
```{r}
get_lengths <- function(l) {
  sapply(l, length)
}
get_lengths(list(1:3, 1:5))
get_lengths(list())

sapply(1:3, function(i) {
  seq_len(i)
})
sapply(1:3, function(i) {
  c(min = i, max = i^2)
})

events <- data.frame(id = 1, start = as.POSIXct("2024-01-01", tz = "UTC"))
sapply(events["id"], class)
sapply(events, class)
```
:::

## Why

`sapply()` applies the function, then tries to simplify the result. If every call returns a single value, you get a vector. If they all return the same number of values, a matrix. Otherwise, a list. And on an empty input there is nothing to simplify: `sapply()` returns `list()`.

The classic `sapply(df, class)` falls into it too. A single column with two classes, such as a date-time (`"POSIXct" "POSIXt"`), is enough to turn the named vector into a list.

So the type of the result depends on the data, not on the code. A function that works on the example breaks further down the line, the day the input is empty or irregular.

## The remedy

`vapply()` makes you declare the shape of each result, and stops if it is not respected.

::: {.piege}
```{r}
get_lengths <- function(l) {
  vapply(l, FUN = length, FUN.VALUE = integer(1))
}
get_lengths(list(1:3, 1:5))
get_lengths(list())

vapply(1:3, FUN = function(i) {
  seq_len(i)
}, FUN.VALUE = integer(1))
```
:::
